chapter: Learning trumpet and first bands in New Orleans
title: Recruited by a Texas band and leaving New Orleans for the first time
summary: Saxophonists Milligan and Baker, with a big Buick and uniforms, offer $30 a week in Texas; he gets his mother's approval, goes, and the boss runs off with a week's pay after four months.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: I said, oh, I don't know. I don't know, man. I don't know. I said, I'd have to talk to my mother about that. And I said, what's the deal? He said, well, we get $30 a week. He said, playing at a nice place. He said, we got a long-term contract. If you'd be interested, say, we've been around them many places and talked to many trumpet players, but we would prefer to have you, because you fit more with the band. And now, man, I fell right in it when I fell in with them, because they liked, you know, for a man to be featured. Because Baker, he played a lot of sax. And he'd feature, you know. Oh yes, he blowed a lot of sax, man. Like Coleman Hawkins, he had to use a mic with that tenor, because he was soft. But when you let him get by that mic, man, he was just like Coleman Hawkins. Big girl. And Bob Milliken was an alto player, but he was loud. He didn't need no mic. Rough. You understand? He was one of them rough players. But I mean, they played all that load. They know just how to make that harmony and everything. And they liked the men to be featured, see. And they said that they had been around many places, but out of all the trumpet players they talked to, they would like to get used. Yeah, you would fit in. You see, because I would fit in with their band, see. They called it their style. Yeah, you see. Oh, they must have had about eight pieces. And so, I told them, I said, well, you'd have to talk to my mom, I don't know, and I ain't made up my mind yet. So them fellas hung around here, man, and they come back to that place three straight nights, trying to get me to make up my mind. So I had talked to my mother in between, you see. And I told them, I said, well, I'll tell you what you do. Well, I think that was on a Tuesday night, the last time they came. I said, now you come by Wednesday evening. I give them my address. I said, I'm right down on Padilla Street. I said, you come by there and I want you to talk to Mama. And you explained it to her just how it is. I said, because I've never been away from here. I said, and she'll have to give it okay. What she say is all right with me. So they say, okay. So at 2 or 2.30, they were right at my door there. So I invited them in the house. I said, come on in. And then I called Mama from the kitchen. She was cooking there. I said, now Mama, I said, these boys want me to go away to four and play with them. I said, now they've got a good job over there. I said, now I believe I'd like to play with them. I said, but it's up to you. I said, because I ain't never been away that far before. See, I thought it was Plum and Nelly, man, you know, one of them strictly New Orleans, you know, catch, you know, just round, yeah. So she listened at them, he talked, and that big car out there might be a brand new. And man, they had the uniforms. You know, see, you know they didn't come in raggedy, because I'd have been scared, see. They had to tell them, say, if you need any loot, say, just what you need.
You thought it was Plum and Nelly?
Yeah, you know, yeah, man. I ain't never been away, man. I never thought I could leave away from here. Well, we went up on the job, man.
And what does Plum and Nelly mean? Some people don't know.

Well, that's just too far, man, when you ain't been there. Plum and Nelly up in Kip. Yeah, yeah, that's just too far when you ain't been there, see. You used that to praise your watchers. Not realize, you know, that you can cross Louisiana and go into Texas and just step across there. But a person that's never left New Orleans, you know, see, man, that's full way, that's way away from here. Oh, yeah. Well, I went on up there, and the job lasted pretty good for four months. See, they had a contract modified signed by the Notre Republic, too. But this man, he run away with all the money one night. One Saturday night, went away with all of them. We didn't get paid for that last week. And I don't know if he ever come back. Yeah, the boss. He went away, just left. Nobody in the way. And his wife said that she couldn't afford to carry that burden, because she didn't like that kind of business, no way. But he wanted to be in it. What was the name of the journey? Oh, similar to the one you had here, Dew Drop, you know. Oh, mm-hmm. Yeah. You know, we were drawing good crowds, man. I liked that band.
